pages.text: The solar system is the sun and everything that orbits it: eight planets, five dwarf planets, more than 200 moons, thousands of comets, and millions of asteroids. It extends from the blazing surface of the sun at its centre to the outer reaches of the Oort Cloud, a vast sphere of icy objects so distant that the most remote of them take millions of years to complete a single orbit.

image.note: Diagram of the solar system showing the sun and eight planets in order, with asteroid belt and Kuiper belt indicated

pages.text: The solar system formed approximately 4.6 billion years ago from a cloud of gas and dust that collapsed under its own gravity. As the cloud contracted, it began to spin. Most of the material fell to the centre, where it became the sun. The rest formed a flat disc around it, and within that disc, particles collided and clumped together to form the planets.

The sun contains more than 99 percent of all the mass in the solar system. Every planet, moon, asteroid, and comet is a tiny fraction of what is left over. The gravitational pull of this enormous mass is what holds all the other objects in their orbits. Without the sun, every planet would fly off into interstellar space in a straight line.

The scale of the solar system defeats the imagination, so try a model. Shrink the sun to the size of a large orange on a table. Earth becomes a grain of sand ten metres away. Jupiter, a peppercorn, sits fifty metres off. Neptune's grain of sand lies three hundred metres distant, out of the room and down the street. Almost all of the solar system is empty space. The planets are rare specks in an enormous, patient dark.

The four planets closest to the sun, Mercury, Venus, Earth, and Mars, are rocky. They are small, dense, and solid. The four outer planets, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune, are giants made primarily of gas and ice. Between the rocky planets and the gas giants lies the asteroid belt, a region of space containing millions of rocky fragments that never coalesced into a planet.

Mercury is the smallest planet and the closest to the sun. Its surface temperature swings between 430 degrees Celsius in the day and minus 180 at night, the most extreme temperature range of any planet. It has no atmosphere to moderate heat and retain warmth. Venus, the next planet out, is the hottest, despite being further from the sun: its thick carbon dioxide atmosphere traps heat in a runaway greenhouse effect.

pages.text: Earth is the only planet known to support life. Its distance from the sun, its size, its magnetic field, its atmosphere, and the presence of liquid water on its surface create conditions that, so far as we know, exist nowhere else in the solar system. Mars, the next planet out, is cold, dry, and thin-atmosphered, but it shows evidence of having had liquid water in the distant past.

Jupiter is the largest planet, so large that all the other planets could fit inside it with room to spare. It has a storm called the Great Red Spot that has been raging for at least 350 years. Saturn is famous for its rings, which are made of billions of pieces of ice and rock. Uranus and Neptune are ice giants, blue-green in colour, cold, and remote. Neptune is so far from the sun that one orbit takes 165 earth years.

Saturn is not the only ringed planet, merely the show-off. Jupiter, Uranus, and Neptune all have faint ring systems, but Saturn's are broad, bright, and made of countless pieces of ice, from dust grains to chunks the size of houses, all orbiting in a disc thinner, in proportion, than a sheet of paper. The rings are probably young and may not last. We happen to be alive at a moment when Saturn wears its crown.

Moons outnumber planets many times over, and the interesting ones may not be planets at all. Jupiter's moon Europa hides a salt-water ocean beneath a crust of ice, kept liquid by the squeeze of Jupiter's gravity. Saturn's moon Titan has rivers and seas, though of liquid methane, not water. If life exists elsewhere in the solar system, some scientists bet it will be found not on a planet but in the dark ocean of a frozen moon.

Beyond Neptune lies the Kuiper Belt, a region of space filled with icy objects, the largest of which is Pluto. Pluto was classified as a planet from its discovery in 1930 until 2006, when it was reclassified as a dwarf planet because it shares its orbital neighbourhood with many similar objects rather than clearing it as the eight planets do.

Beyond the Kuiper Belt lies the Oort Cloud, a vast and still largely theoretical sphere of icy bodies surrounding the solar system at enormous distance. Comets, which are icy bodies that develop bright tails of gas and dust when they approach the sun, originate in the Kuiper Belt and the Oort Cloud. When their orbits are disturbed, perhaps by a passing star, they fall inward toward the sun and become briefly spectacular before either returning to the outer solar system or being destroyed.

pages.text: The Voyager 1 spacecraft, launched in 1977, is now the most distant human-made object in existence. It has left the solar system and is travelling through interstellar space. It carries a golden record containing sounds and images from earth, chosen to represent life and culture on our planet to any intelligent civilisation that might one day find it. Voyager 1 will not reach the nearest star for approximately 40,000 years.

Comets are the solar system's messengers from the deep freeze. Made of ice, dust, and rock, they spend most of their lives in the frozen outer reaches. When one falls sunward, the sun's heat boils off gas and dust into a glowing tail that can stretch across the sky. Ancient peoples read comets as omens. We now read them as time capsules, carrying material unchanged since the solar system was born, which spacecraft have flown out to sample directly.

Nigeria has a National Space Research and Development Agency, established in 1999. It has launched several satellites, including the NigeriaSat series, which provide images used in mapping, monitoring environmental change, and supporting agriculture. Nigeria is one of the African countries most actively investing in space technology.

Africa as a whole is increasingly engaged in space science. The Square Kilometre Array, the largest radio telescope ever built, has a major component in South Africa. African astronomers are contributing to discoveries about the universe from observatories across the continent. Space science is not remote from Africa. It is something Africa is helping to build.

For anyone growing up in Nigeria today, space is both overhead and ahead. The satellites that help map Niger Delta oil spills, monitor desertification in the north, and predict weather patterns for farmers are overhead, circling the earth right now. The careers that will build Nigeria's next generation of space technology are still ahead, waiting for the people who will choose them.

pages.text: Africa is looking up. Nigeria's space agency operates Earth-observation satellites that track flooding, monitor farmland, and map the advancing desert. Across the continent, new observatories, university programmes, and the giant Square Kilometre Array in South Africa are pulling African scientists to the front of astronomy. Space is not a rich country's hobby. It is a tool for solving problems on the ground, and the next generation to use it well may be reading this page.
